transcript.text:
The high country around Greyhollow is old and hard: grey peaks that hold their snow nearly the year round, pine valleys strung with mine roads, and beneath the stone a web of workings older than anyone living can remember. The town itself is cut into the mountainside, its streets steep and sheltered from the wind, and over it all the temple of the Anvil Father keeps its fires burning, as it has for as long as there have been miners to go down into the dark.

Brakka Ironvein has served six years as a guard at that temple — a hill dwarf with a smith's hands and an acolyte's vows, more used to a quiet watch than to fear. Now the town is afraid. Three days ago three miners went down into the old north workings, sealed a generation ago, and none came back. Last night a fourth man came up alone, babbling of lights that walk, and died before dawn. The council has had enough: at sunrise tomorrow they will brick up the mine mouth, missing men or no.

That is why Brakka stands now at the mine entrance in the late afternoon, a hooded lantern from the temple in one hand, the cold wind at his back. Prior Hessa asked him to go down before sunrise and bring back whoever can still be brought back. The dark mouth of the workings waits, sealed timber wrenched aside, a faint draught of old, cold air breathing out of it.

What do you do?

I check the ground around the mine mouth for tracks before going in, looking for the miners' boot prints and anything that might have come out. Then I light the hooded lantern, loosen my sword in its sheath, and tie off a length of rope at the entrance so I can find my way back.

You go to one knee and read the trampled earth, and it tells you plainly. Three heavy boot-prints, three days old and gone soft at the edges, go in through the mouth side by side — the lost miners. A fourth, smaller and a little later, follows them in alone. Then, coming back out last night, a single set: a staggering line, toes dug deep, a hand- and knee-print where the man fell and hauled himself up again, dried black drop-spots between. By the end the prints are near-bare, and you know it was him — the fourth miner, walking out of the dark.

There is one thing more. Just within the threshold's shadow the dust lies in a shape that is no boot: a narrow footfall without a heel, and it still holds a failing light, a dim phosphor like spilled moonlight, already fading. It points back into the workings.

The lantern's tank is full — the temple saw to that. You raise the wick and the flame catches, throwing bright light thirty feet and dim light beyond. You loosen the sword in its sheath, draw the rope out, and make it fast to one of the wrenched timbers, ready to pay it out behind you as you go.

What do you do?

I crouch over the glowing heelless print for a moment, studying how far apart the steps are and whether anything seems to have dragged. Then I mutter a quick prayer to the Anvil Father, shift my shield to my arm, and start into the workings, paying out rope and keeping the lantern low and forward.

You crouch over the print a moment longer. Its light is nearly gone now, and there is only the one clear mark — the rest too faint to hold, or never there. Whatever set it trod lightly; there is no scrape, no drag, no heel. It went inward, and it did not linger.

You murmur a prayer to the Anvil Father, settle the shield on your arm, and step into the workings, the lantern low and forward, the rope paying out behind you.

The drift is wide and square-cut, braced by old timbers gone slack with age, a rusted rail down its middle. The air is cold and dead, smelling of dust and old iron, and your footfalls and the soft grind of the rope are the only sounds. The dust on the floor tells the tale again: three men in, one out.

The drift runs level and straight a good while, then begins to slope down, its braces set closer, its floor roughened by the years. There is a chalk arrow on one timber, a miner's mark, three days old, pointing on. Before long your rope runs to its end, and you knot the free end high on a bracing and go on, keeping to the single passage.

The slope levels into a low chamber, the roof sagging between its timbers. Along one wall three miners' candles have burned down to stubs and gone cold. And along the floor, here and there, that same faint luminous dust, in a thin, wandering trail that leads toward a side-passage on your left — black as ink even to the lantern's light.

I check the cold candle stubs and the floor around them for anything the miners left behind, like tools, packs, or more chalk marks. Then I follow the glowing trail to the mouth of the left passage, stopping there to listen before I go in.

You search the stubs and the floor around them, and the miners' pause comes back to you piece by piece. The three candles stand in a row along the wall, their wax pooled and cold, burned right down until they guttered out. Propped against the timber is a miner's pick, its handle wrapped with a frayed strip of cloth. Near it a canvas shoulder-bag has toppled and spilled: a handful of iron pitons, a twist of hard twine, a broken whetstone, a dry crust of bread, and an empty tin flask lying on its side. Chalk marks run on the chamber wall — a clear arrow pointing on down the main drift, and, scrawled over the mouth of the side-passage, a rough X with a single dwarven rune beside it, the one for danger.

You move to the side-passage's black mouth and stand still, listening. The workings are quiet as a tomb — and then, far down the passage, so faint you almost take it for your own blood in your ears, a soft and even sound comes and goes: something like light footfalls, or the slow drip of water in a hollow, a long way off. Then silence.

What do you do?

I pocket the pitons and twine, since they might be useful, and leave the pick where it lies. The miners marked that passage as danger and the main drift as the way on, but the glowing trail goes left, so I'll stay out of the side-passage for now and look down the main drift first. I want to see whether the three men kept going that way before I walk into whatever is making that sound.

You pocket the pitons and the twist of twine and leave the pick against the timber — let it lie where courage faltered. Then you step clear of the side-passage and look down the main drift, holding the lantern forward.

The dust tells it plainly. Three sets of boot-prints, three days old, go on down the drift together, and a single set returns from the deep, the fourth man's, staggering back the way he came. No phosphor dust here — the glowing trail belongs to the side-passage alone. Whatever the miners found, they found it down the main drift.

The drift slopes away into solid dark, the air a little warmer now as it descends. Some thirty feet on, the lantern's light catches a faint glint low on the railbed — something small and metal, dropped in the dust.

What do you do?
I walk the thirty feet carefully, watching the floor for anything odd, and crouch to look at the glint before touching it. If it's safe, I pick it up and see what it is.

Step by step you cross the thirty feet, and the floor underfoot is honest mine-work gone soft with age: crumbled flakes of timber, loose scree, the rusted rail cold through the dust. Nothing shifts, nothing gives way. You find no trip, no wire, no trick.

It lies where the fourth man's returning prints are scuffed and turned, as if he dropped it in his haste and never stooped to take it up again. The metal is cold, lightly dented, but sound.

You take it up and the drift waits, sloping on into the dark before you.

I tuck the whistle into my belt pouch and slip the broken thong in after it, then check the dust around where the fourth man's prints turned for any blood or sign of what made him run. After that I keep following the three sets of boot-prints down the drift, lantern held forward.

You tuck the whistle and its broken thong into your belt pouch, then go over the turned prints again, close this time.

Here the blood is heavier and closer-set, black and long dried, some of it smeared where a hand was pressed and lifted. The stride lengthens as it goes on — no stagger now but a full run, the toes driving. A few paces back toward the deep lie two or three smears of that same luminous dust, now gone nearly dark on the stone: the lights came into the drift after him a little way, and then drew off. The air here holds a faint smell, scorched dust and something cold and keen, the smell that hangs in the air before lightning.

You leave that place and follow the three sets of prints on down, the lantern before you. The drift drops by long slopes and turns, the timber braces thinning out until they give way to raw rock; the rusted rail ended long ago. Water beads the walls and patters somewhere out of sight. The three prints press on and on, and the smell grows warmer.

After a good while the drift levels, and the lantern-light spills into a wide gallery. Here the three sets of prints no longer run straight: they scatter and cross and double back in the dust, a milling, boots turning every way at once, all of it three days old. Across the far side of the trampled floor the rock is streaked black, as if scorched.

I stop at the edge of the gallery and sweep the lantern across the floor and walls before stepping onto the trampled ground. Then I look closely at the scorched streaks on the far side, checking whether the burning looks like lightning, fire, or something else, and whether the prints lead toward them or away.

You stop at the edge of the trampled ground and sweep the lantern slowly across the gallery. It is wide and low, its walls water-worn, the drift giving over to it; the scorched rock waits at the far side. The lantern's light falls short of the corners, and the dark there keeps its business to itself, but nothing moves within the reach of the flame.

You cross to the scorched rock and study it close. It is no smith's soot, no woodsmoke. The burns branch and fork across the stone like old blood-veins, and where they run the rock is fused to a thin, glassy skin — hotter and stranger than fire, an etching you know only from storm-season tales. Lightning.

The burns all crown one place: a ragged, vertical crack in the rock, hung at its edges with fresh pick-scars where someone once widened it. Black as a closed eye, it opens from the floor to above a man's head, shoulder-wide at the middle.

And the boot-prints settle the rest. The three sets mill and cross, then come together and go straight for that crack; at its very mouth they are heaviest, and there they are blotted out and gone, and no three sets come away. Only the fourth man's turn and run, back the way you came. A faint draught, cold and steady, moves against your lantern-flame, and it breathes out of the crack itself.

I hold the lantern near the crack and look at the fresh pick-scars and the edges for any sign of what's inside, and I listen at it for a moment. Then I tie the twine and a piton into a makeshift line anchor at the crack's mouth so I have a marker back, and call softly into it for the miners by name if I can recall them from Hessa's account.

Close in, the crack tells more. The pick-scars are three days fresh, their edges crisp, the work of strong and practised hands. The glassy scorch is deepest at the very mouth — the lightning came out of the dark within and licked the rock as it went. Low on one lip there is a dried black handprint, a man's, fingers spread, and beside it scuffed drag-lines in the dust, as if someone had been hauled on hands and knees over that threshold. A few strands of wool are snagged on the cut edge where a sleeve tore.

You set your ear against the cold rock and hold your breath, and you hear only the slow deep drip and the single heavy note of your own blood. The crack gives nothing else up.

So you jam a piton into the crack's jaw and bind the twine's end around it, leaving the line to mark your way back. Then you put your mouth to the opening and call the names Hessa laid out for you — Borrin, Alda, Kell — one after another into the dark.

The names go down and come back hollow and far. And on the last of them, from deep and deep below, a single slow scraping sound replies, like iron dragged over stone, once, and then the cold draught breathes once against your face and is still.

RULE Creature Size:
Each creature takes up a different amount of space. The Size Categories table shows how much space a creature of a particular size controls in combat. Objects sometimes use the same size categories.

#### Size Categories

| Size       | Space                  |
|------------|------------------------|
| Tiny       | 2.5 by 2.5 ft.           |
| Small      | 5 by 5 ft.             |
| Medium     | 5 by 5 ft.             |
| Large      | 10 by 10 ft.           |
| Huge       | 15 by 15 ft.           |
| Gargantuan | 20 by 20 ft. or larger |

#### Space

A creature's space is the area in feet that it effectively controls in combat, not an expression of its physical dimensions. A typical Medium creature isn't 5 feet wide, for example, but it does control a space that wide. If a Medium hobgoblin stands in a 5-foot-wide doorway, other creatures can't get through unless the hobgoblin lets them.

A creature's space also reflects the area it needs to fight effectively. For that reason, there's a limit to the number of creatures that can surround another creature in combat. Assuming Medium combatants, eight creatures can fit in a 5-foot radius around another one.

Because larger creatures take up more space, fewer of them can surround a creature. If five Large creatures crowd around a Medium or smaller one, there's little room for anyone else. In contrast, as many as twenty Medium creatures can surround a Gargantuan one.

#### Squeezing into a Smaller Space

A creature can squeeze through a space that is large enough for a creature one size smaller than it. Thus, a Large creature can squeeze through a passage that's only 5 feet wide. While squeezing through a space, a creature must spend 1 extra foot for every foot it moves there, and it has disadvantage on attack rolls and Dexterity saving throws. Attack rolls against the creature have advantage while it's in the smaller space.

story.text:
**STORY SO FAR — recap for continuity (turns 0–4, plus state through turn 9)**

**World & setup**
- Calendar: 12 months × 30 days (Deepwinter, Thaw, Sowing, Rains, Blossom, Highsun, Midsummer, Haying, Harvest, Leaffall, Frost, Yearsend). Game opened on **Day 1, the 20th of Frost, 714**, at 4:30 PM. Time now **5:23 PM**.
- The region: high, cold mining country around **Greyhollow**, a mining town cut into a grey mountainside. Over it sits the **Temple of the Anvil Father**, whose prior is **Hessa** (an old dwarf). The god **the Anvil Father** is patron of smiths, mines, honest toil.
- **Brakka Ironvein** (hill dwarf, fighter 1, acolyte) served six years as a guard at that temple. HP 14/14, AC 18, passive Perception 14, darkvision 60 ft, dwarven resilience (poison), etc.

**The opening problem (canon, fixed)**
- Three days ago (the 17th of Frost), three miners went down into the **old north workings** of the **Greyhollow mine** — a section sealed a generation ago — and none came back.
- Last night (night of the 19th/20th) a fourth man came up alone babbling about **lights that walk**, and died before dawn today (the 20th).
- The **town council** will brick up the mine entrance at **sunrise tomorrow (the 21st)** regardless.
- Prior Hessa asked Brakka to go down before then and bring back whoever can still be brought back.

**The three miners' names (established turn 8, given by Hessa): Borrin, Alda, Kell.** The fourth (dead) miner is **Osric**. Hessa gave Brakka all four names.

**Items Brakka carries (current):** Chain Mail, Longsword, Shield, Crossbow light, Crossbow bolts ×20, Backpack, Bedroll, Mess kit, Tinderbox, Torch ×10, Rations ×10, Waterskin, Hempen rope 50 ft, Holy symbol of the Anvil Father, Prayer book, Stick of incense ×5, Vestments, Common clothes, Belt pouch, Hooded lantern (borrowed, lit), Pitons ×5 (6 originally, 1 used as anchor), Signal whistle (found), plus 15 gp. **Twine is gone** (used as marker line). No oil flask carried — the borrowed lantern was said to be filled by the temple ("the temple saw to it"); its timer started at 6 hours (lit at 4:30 PM).

**Key established mechanics/facts**
- Lantern lit at 4:30 PM; 6-hour oil timer runs to 10:30 PM. (Lantern: bright 30 ft, dim to 60 ft.)
- A **hempen rope** was tied at the mine mouth, paid out 50 ft, then the end knotted high on a timber partway when it ran out.

**What happened, in order**

1. **At the mine mouth**: Brakka read the ground — natural 20 Survival check. Revealed: three boot-prints going in three days ago; a fourth set slightly later going in alone; one staggering, near-barefoot set coming out last night with dried black blood drop-spots (the fourth man, Osric). **Discovery (natural 20):** just inside the threshold, in the dust, a single fading luminous footfall narrow and without a heel, pointing inward — the mark of **the walking lights**.
2. **Entering**: worked square-cut drift, rusted rail, cold dead air; chalk arrow on a timber pointing on. Rope ran out and was knotted off.
3. **The low chamber**: roof sagging; three miners' candle stubs burned out; a miner's pick (handle wrapped in cloth) left against the wall; a spilled canvas bag (pitons, hard twine, broken whetstone, dry crust, empty tin flask); chalk — an arrow on down the main drift, and over the **side-passage** a rough X with the dwarven rune for **danger**. A faint luminous dust trail led toward the side-passage on the left. Brakka listened (Perception success) — faint far sound, like footfalls or dripping, from the side-passage.
4. **Brakka's choices in the low chamber**: pocketed **6 pitons and the twine**; left the pick. He decided the side-passage was marked danger, and chose to follow the **main drift** where the chalk arrow pointed.
5. **Following the main drift**: three sets of boot-prints (three days old) going down together; one set (Osric's) returning, staggering. No luminous dust on the main-drift floor — the dust trail belongs to the side-passage only.
6. **The glint**: ~30 ft down, metal in the dust — a **miner's signal whistle**, steel, thong snapped, lying where Osric's returning prints scuffed and turned. Brakka pocketed it (thong too).
7. **Blood/spoor at Osric's turn**: heavier, closer-set dried black blood, smeared (hand pressed to a wound); his stride becomes a flat-out run. A few darkening luminous dust-smears a few paces behind his line — the lights pursued him a little way into the drift, then drew off. Smell: scorched dust + cold keen smell "like before lightning."
8. **The deep gallery** (deep end of the main drift): wide, low, water-worn room; timber braces long gone, raw rock; floor trampled — three sets of prints mill, cross, double back. Far wall rock streaked black/scorched.

**Turn 4 ended here** — Brakka had just reached the deep gallery and the trampled/scorched scene, with the milled prints and scorched far wall, not yet examined closely.

**Turns 5–9 since (state to carry forward):**

9. **Examining the gallery** (Perception sweep DC 12 **failed with a 7**; Investigation of scorch DC 13 **hit exactly, 13**): The scorch is **not fire/soot but branching, glassy-fused lightning burns** — an etching like storm-damage. The gallery's corners stayed beyond lantern reach (nothing seen there). The burns crown a **ragged vertical natural crack** — the **scorched fissure** — floor to above head-height, shoulder-wide, hung with **fresh three-days-old pick-scars** (the miners had widened it — a hint that the workings were sealed a generation ago because they broke into this natural deep). At its mouth the three sets of prints are heaviest and then blotted out — no three sets return; only Osric's turns and bolts back the way he came. A cold steady draught breathes out of the crack.
10. **Close examination** (Perception 22) revealed: the lightning came from *within* the crack (heaviest scorch at the mouth); a dried black **handprint** low on one lip; scuffed drag-lines (someone hauled on hands and knees over the threshold); wool strands snagged where a sleeve tore.
11. **Listening** at the crack (Perception DC 15 **failed, 10**): only the drip and his own blood; nothing else heard.
12. **Anchor**: Brakka jammed a **piton** into the crack's jaw and tied the **twine** to it as a back-marker (Pitons now ×5; Twine consumed).
13. **Calling** the names Borrin, Alda, Kell into the dark: a single **slow scraping sound** (like iron dragged over stone) answered from deep below, once; draught breathed once.
14. **Waiting, then a quieter call** (announcing Prior Hessa sent him from the Anvil Father's temple, come to bring them home): far down in the crack, a **pale cold light fluttered once** (the color of the fading dust) and went out; a thread-thin word answered, uncertain — "cold" or "come"; then silence and the draught.

**What Brakka knows/decides:** the side-passage is marked danger and avoided for now; the three miners and Osric went down the main drift; the lightning-scorched fissure is where the men's prints end and where the walking lights seem to dwell; something down there answers his calls with faint light and a scraped/voiced sound.

**Open threads:** find Borrin, Alda, Kell (and any survivors); the nature of the walking lights (lightning-related, luminous dust, pursued Osric); why the workings were sealed a generation ago (likely they'd broken into the natural deeps); the town council's sunrise deadline (the 21st). The side-passage (marked danger, faint sound) is still unexplored. The low chamber's pick and gear left behind.

**Decisions made but not yet revealed in play:**
- The walking lights are associated with **lightning** damage (scorched, branching, glassy, ozone-like smell). If/when statted, must fit a solo level-1 PC — a full will-o'-wisp (CR 2) is too strong unless carefully handled; treat as a severe threat, likely requiring avoidance, cleverness, or very careful balance rather than a straight brawl.
- The deeps behind the fissure are a natural cave network the old miners broke into a generation ago, which is why the workings were sealed.
- The miners' fate is not yet shown: dried blood, drag-marks, and a torn sleeve suggest one was struck/pulled at the fissure; blotted prints suggest the three were taken or drawn inside rather than walking out.
- Osric's injuries: he bled badly, fled on foot, and died before dawn from what he found — the cause of death not yet established (could be wounds, fright, or the lightning).

**STORY SO FAR — continuity recap (turns 0–11, plus the ongoing fight state at turn 16)**

**World & clock**
- Calendar: 12 months × 30 days (Deepwinter, Thaw, Sowing, Rains, Blossom, Highsun, Midsummer, Haying, Harvest, Leaffall, Frost, Yearsend). Game opened on **Day 1, the 20th of Frost, 714**, at 4:30 PM. End of turn 11: **5:27 PM**.
- Setting: high, cold mining country around **Greyhollow**, a town cut into a grey mountainside. Over it, the **Temple of the Anvil Father**; its prior is **Hessa** (old dwarf). The god **the Anvil Father** is patron of smiths, mines, honest toil (the temple's fires watch over the miners).
- **Brakka Ironvein** (hill dwarf fighter 1, acolyte) served six years as a temple guard there. STR 15, DEX 10, CON 16, INT 8, WIS 14, CHA 12; AC 18 (chain mail + shield); HP 14/14 max; speed 25; prof +2. Longsword +4 (1d8+4, Dueling) or 1d10+2 two-handed; light crossbow +2 (1d8); Second Wind 1/1 (heals 1d10+1); passive Perception 14; darkvision 60 ft; Dwarven Resilience (adv. poison saves, resist poison); Stonecunning. Skills: Athletics +4, Insight +4, Perception +4, Religion +1. Languages: Common, Dwarvish, Giant, Goblin. XP 0/300. Money 15 gp.

**The opening problem (fixed)**
- Three days ago (the 17th of Frost) three miners — **Borrin, Alda, Kell** — went down into the **old north workings**, a section of the Greyhollow mine sealed a generation ago, and none came back.
- Last night (19th→20th) a fourth man, **Osric**, came up alone babbling about **lights that walk**, and died before dawn today (the 20th).
- The **town council** will brick up the mine entrance at **sunrise tomorrow (the 21st)** regardless.
- Prior Hessa asked Brakka to go down before then and bring back whoever can still be brought back; she gave him all four names.

**Story in order (turns 0–11)**
1. **Mine mouth (turn 1):** natural 20 Survival — three boot-prints going in three days ago; a fourth set going in alone; one staggering, near-barefoot set coming out (Osric's) with dried black blood drop-spots. Natural-20 discovery: a single fading luminous, narrow, heel-less footfall in the dust just inside, pointing inward — mark of the walking lights. Lit the lantern, tied rope at the entrance.
2. **Entering (turn 2):** square-cut drift, rusted rail, cold dead air, chalk arrow on a timber. Rope pays out (50 ft, then knotted off).
3. **The low chamber (turns 3–4):** sagging roof; three burned-out candle stubs; a miner's pick (cloth-wrapped handle) against the wall; a spilled bag (pitons, hard twine, broken whetstone, dry crust, empty tin flask); chalk arrow on down the main drift and a rough X with the dwarven "danger" rune over a **side-passage**; a faint luminous dust trail toward that side-passage; faint far sound (footfalls/dripping) from it. Brakka pocketed 6 pitons and the twine, left the pick, chose the marked-danger side route to AVOID, and followed the main drift.
4. **Main drift (turns 5–6):** three sets of boot-prints (three days old) going down; one set (Osric) returning. No luminous dust on the main floor. Found a **steel miner's signal whistle** (thong snapped) where Osric's prints turned (turn 5). At Osric's turn: heavier, closer-set black blood (hand pressed to a wound), stride becomes a full run; a few darkening luminous dust-smears a few paces behind his line (the lights pursued him a little, then drew off); smell of scorched dust + the cold, keen "before-lightning" smell.
5. **The deep gallery (turn 6–7):** wide, low, water-worn room; timbers gone to raw rock; three sets of prints mill, cross, double back; far wall streaked black/scorched. Perception (7, fail) for a corner sweep; Investigation (13, exact hit): the scorch is **not fire but branching, glassy-fused lightning burns** — crown a ragged, vertical **scorched fissure** (floor to above head-high, shoulder-wide at the middle, hung with three-days-fresh pick-scars). Boot-prints come together and go straight for it, heaviest at its mouth, blotted out there; no three sets come away — only Osric's turns and runs back. A cold, steady draught breathes out of the crack.
6. **The fissure (turn 8):** Perception 22 — the lightning came from **within** (heaviest scorch at the mouth); a dried black **handprint** low on one lip; scuffed drag-lines (someone hauled over the threshold on hands and knees); wool strands snagged where a sleeve tore. Listen (10, fail): only the drip. Brakka jammed a **piton** into the crack's jaw and tied the **twine** to it as back-marker (pitons 6→5, twine consumed).
7. **Calling (turns 8–9):** calling Borrin, Alda, Kell into the dark → a single slow **scraping sound** (iron dragged over stone) answered once from deep below. A quieter call (Prior Hessa sent me, come to bring you home) → far down, a **pale cold light** fluttered once (color of the fading dust) and went out; a thread-thin word answered, "cold" or "come."
8. **Entering the deeps (turn 10):** Perception 21 — the crack's mouth is shoulder-wide, edges fused glassy-black; beyond it a natural water-carved passage descends, the scorch running along it like veins of black glass; the cold draught pours up it. Judged himself through sideways in armor. (Created **the natural deeps**.)
9. **Descending (turn 11):** no twine left to pay out (spent) and the rope lies far behind (deployed from the mine mouth). Perception 18 — scorch veins thickest where the lightning lingered (as though the light moved down this way); faint smears of cold luminous dust going down ahead like a trail of starlight; far below, a pale light "breathes once — and holds."

**Where things stand at end of turn 11:** Brakka is inside the **natural deeps**, a water-carved cave network behind the fissure, descending toward a pale light at the limit of sight, on a trail of luminous dust. The twine marks the crack behind him; the rope is strung toward the mine mouth.

Links: Temple inside Greyhollow; old north workings inside Greyhollow mine; Greyhollow mine adjoining Greyhollow; low chamber and deep gallery inside old north workings; scorched fissure adjoining deep gallery AND adjoining the natural deeps.

**Fight state (turn 16, ongoing):** No fight was on until turn 16. Brakka opened the lantern full, stepped between the light and the miners, drew steel, attacked. **Combatants:** Brakka Ironvein (initiative 13) and "the walking light" (initiative 8). Round 1: Brakka missed (9 vs AC 15); the light hit him with its cold touch for **3 cold damage** (Brakka now **11/14 HP**). Now **Round 2, Brakka's turn**. The light is 16/16 HP, AC 15, hovering in front of him. Kell and Alda are behind/adjacent nearby in the low stone pocket.

**The creature ("the walking light") — a custom, WEAKENED will-o'-wisp** (NOT the full CR 2 SRD stat block; a faded/young one, balanced for a solo level-1 PC): man-shaped, tall and thin, narrow heel-less feet, featureless bright face. AC 15; HP 16; fly 30 ft (hover). Attack "cold touch": +4 to hit, reach 5 ft, **1d6+2 cold** damage (draws warmth, "goes in through the skin"). Damage immunities: lightning, poison; resistance: cold (NOT resistant to nonmagical B/P/S, so Brakka's steel works). Condition immunities as a wisp (exhaustion, grappled, paralyzed, poisoned, prone, restrained, unconscious). Traits (may matter): Incorporeal Movement (pass through creatures/objects as difficult terrain), Variable Illumination (bonus action to brighten/dim light), and Consume Life (bonus action: a 0-HP living creature within 5 ft must DC 10 Con save or die; on death the light regains 3d6 HP). Resolve its turns MANUALLY (next_turn + roll + change_creature/change_pc), not via creature_turns, since it has no SRD stat block matched.

**Decisions made that are now established in play (keep consistent):**
- The **walking lights** are lightning-linked, cold, leave luminous dust, walk on narrow heel-less feet; the scorch came from within the deeps.
- **Borrin** went deeper after the light; "the light is in him," "gone all lit up inside" (taken/possessed).
- **Kell** is alive but half-frozen, unable to walk ("cold's got into my legs, into my hands"), sitting against the wall.
- **Alda** lies cold beside Kell, "won't wake" (unconscious/or worse — not yet settled).
- The lone man-shaped figure is a faded will-o'-wisp whose strength is spent into the scorching and into Borrin.

**Open threads:** rescue Borrin, Alda, Kell; the nature of the walking lights; why the workings were sealed a generation ago (they'd broken into the natural deeps); the council's sunrise deadline (the 21st); the danger-marked side-passage still unexplored; the low chamber's pick and gear left behind; Osric's cause of death unestablished.

sheet.opening: Brakka Ironvein served six years as a guard at the Temple of the Anvil Father in Greyhollow, a mining town cut into a cold mountainside. Three days ago three miners went down into the old north workings, which were sealed a generation ago, and none came back. Last night a fourth man came up out of the dark alone, babbling about lights that walk, then died before dawn. It is late afternoon, and Brakka stands at the mine mouth with a lantern borrowed from the temple.
